Summary: Terah took his son Abram, his grandson Lot, and his daughter-in-law Sarai out of Ur of the Chaldees to go to Canaan, but the family stopped and settled in Haran, where Terah died. This journey sets up Abraham's later call: the family left Ur but did not reach Canaan in Terah's lifetime.
Significance: The journey shows a partial obedience that God then completes through Abraham's call from Haran.

Journey: Abraham's Journey from Ur to Canaan
Summary: After Terah's death, God called Abram to leave Haran for a land God would show him. Abram traveled with Sarai and Lot through Shechem and Bethel, building altars as he went, and settled in the hill country near Hebron. The route stages named here are those Genesis names; the text does not trace every stop between them.
Significance: The founding migration of Israel's story: leaving home on a promise, not a map, becomes the pattern of faith in Hebrews 11.

Journey: Abram's Journey to Egypt and Back
Summary: When famine struck Canaan, Abram went down into Egypt to live there for a time. After Pharaoh sent him away, Abram returned to Bethel, to the place where his tent and altar had been at the beginning. The text does not name the Egyptian town where he stayed, so none is given as a stage.
Significance: The journey exposes Abram's fear and failure alongside God's protection of the promise, and it previews Israel's later sojourn in Egypt.

Summary: After returning from Egypt, Abram and Lot's herdsmen quarreled because the land could not support both households. Abram let Lot choose first; Lot chose the well-watered plain of the Jordan toward Sodom, while Abram settled in the land of Canaan near Hebron. The stages give each man's destination, not a shared road.
Significance: The parting shows Abram trusting God's promise rather than grabbing the best land, and it places Lot on the road toward Sodom's judgment.

Stages: Hebron; Beer Lahai Roi; Beersheba; Wilderness of Paran
Summary: Hagar first fled from Sarai's harsh treatment and met the angel of the LORD by a spring on the way to Shur, at Beer Lahai Roi, then returned. Years later, after Isaac's birth, Abraham sent Hagar and Ishmael away with bread and water; they wandered in the wilderness of Beersheba and then lived in the wilderness of Paran. The two departures are combined here because both trace Hagar's forced journeys; the text does not name every stop.
Significance: God sees and provides for the outcast: Hagar names God El Roi, the God who sees, and Ishmael's line is preserved by promise.

Journey: Lot's Escape from Sodom to Zoar
Summary: Warned by two angels, Lot fled Sodom at dawn with his wife and two daughters, escaping to the small town of Zoar as fire fell on the cities of the plain. Lot's wife looked back and became a pillar of salt, so only Lot and his daughters reached Zoar. The text gives no intermediate stops.
Significance: The escape is a warning about lingering near judgment and about looking back after being told to flee.

Summary: Abraham sent his steward to his own kindred to find a wife for Isaac. The servant traveled to the city of Nahor in Mesopotamia, prayed at the well, met Rebekah, and brought her back to Isaac in Canaan. The text names the destination region rather than each stop, so only the endpoints are given as stages.
Significance: The mission shows God's guidance through prayer and providence in an ordinary errand, and it secures the promised line through Isaac.

Journey: Isaac's Move to Gerar and Beersheba
Summary: During a famine Isaac went to Gerar in Philistine country rather than down to Egypt. After disputes over wells and a covenant with Abimelech, Isaac moved on and settled at Beersheba, where God renewed the promise made to Abraham. The starting point in Canaan is not named as a town, so the stages begin at Gerar.
Significance: Isaac inherits the promise not by conquest but by digging wells, keeping peace, and trusting God's presence in disputed ground.

Summary: Fleeing Esau's anger, Jacob left Beersheba for Haran to find a wife from Laban's family. At Bethel he dreamed of a ladder reaching to heaven and heard God's promise renewed. He then reached Haran, where he served Laban and married Leah and Rachel. The text names Bethel as the one stop on the way.
Significance: Bethel turns a fugitive's flight into a covenant encounter: God meets Jacob before Jacob has anything to offer.

Stages: Haran; Mahanaim; Penuel; Succoth; Shechem; Bethel; Hebron
Summary: After twenty years with Laban, Jacob left Haran with his wives, children, and flocks. He met angels at Mahanaim, wrestled with God at Penuel and was named Israel, made peace with Esau, built booths at Succoth, camped at Shechem, worshipped at Bethel, and finally reached his father Isaac at Hebron. The stages follow Genesis's own place names in order.
Significance: The return journey is Jacob's transformation in motion: the schemer becomes Israel through wrestling, reconciliation, and worship.

Summary: Jacob sent Joseph from Hebron to check on his brothers grazing near Shechem; a man directed him on to Dothan, where his brothers stripped him, threw him in a pit, and sold him to Ishmaelite traders. The caravan carried him down into Egypt, where he was sold to Potiphar. The text names no Egyptian town of arrival, so Egypt itself is the final stage.
Significance: Joseph's descent begins the chain by which God will later preserve the whole family in famine.

Journey: Jacob's Sons' Grain Journeys to Egypt
Summary: During the famine Jacob sent his sons down to Egypt twice to buy grain, the second time with Benjamin. On the first trip Joseph, unrecognized, held Simeon and demanded Benjamin; on the second, Judah pleaded for Benjamin and Joseph revealed himself. The two trips are combined here because they share one route and one purpose; the text names no stops between Canaan and Egypt.
Significance: The grain road becomes the road to repentance: the brothers who sold Joseph must now stand for Benjamin.

Summary: At God's word Jacob took his whole household down to Egypt, stopping at Beersheba to offer sacrifices, where God assured him in a vision. Joseph met him in Goshen, and Pharaoh settled the family in the land of Goshen. The text names Beersheba as the one stop on the way.
Significance: Israel enters Egypt as a family of seventy and will leave as a nation: descent and deliverance are one story.

Summary: During a famine in Judah, Elimelech took Naomi and their two sons from Bethlehem to live in Moab. Elimelech and both sons died there, and Naomi returned to Bethlehem years later with her daughter-in-law Ruth. The text names no stops on either leg of the journey.
Significance: A famine move meant to save a family empties it instead, and sets up Ruth's loyalty and the road back to Bethlehem.

Summary: After killing an Egyptian and learning Pharaoh sought his life, Moses fled Egypt and sat down by a well in Midian, where he defended Jethro's daughters, married Zipporah, and became a shepherd. The text names no stops on the flight itself.
Significance: Forty years in Midian strip the prince of Egypt down to a shepherd God can send back.

Summary: At the burning bush God sent Moses back to Egypt, and Aaron met him at the mountain of God on the way. Together they gathered Israel's elders and told them God's words, and the people believed. The mountain meeting is the one named stop; Aaron joins Moses en route rather than starting with him.
Significance: The return reverses the flight: the fugitive goes back carrying God's name and his brother's voice.

Journey: Jethro's Visit to Moses at Mount Sinai
Summary: After hearing what God had done in the exodus, Jethro brought Moses's wife Zipporah and his sons to Moses at the mountain of God in the wilderness. Jethro rejoiced, offered sacrifices, and advised Moses to share the burden of judging the people. The text names no stops on the way.
Significance: An outsider's visit brings worship and wise counsel: Jethro blesses God and helps organize Israel's justice.

Stages: Rameses; Succoth; Etham; Migdol; Pi-hahiroth; Red Sea
Summary: After the Passover, Israel left Rameses, camped at Succoth and Etham, then turned back to encamp before Pi-hahiroth between Migdol and the sea. Pharaoh's army pursued them, and God parted the sea so Israel crossed on dry ground while the Egyptians drowned. Debate note: scholars debate the exact locations of several of these stations and the sea crossing itself; the stages given here are the names Exodus uses, in Exodus's order, without fixing modern identifications.
Significance: The exodus is Israel's defining deliverance and the pattern of redemption the rest of Scripture keeps retelling.
RelatedStories: The Exodus and the Red Sea

Stages: Red Sea; Wilderness of Sin; Rephidim; Mount Sinai; Kibroth-hattaavah; Hazeroth; Kadesh Barnea; Mount Hor; Zalmonah; Punon; Oboth; Dibon; Plains of Moab
Scripture: Exodus 15:22-27; Exodus 17:1-16; Exodus 19:1-25; Numbers 10:11-36; Numbers 13:1-33; Numbers 20:1-29; Numbers 21:1-35; Numbers 33:1-49
Summary: From the Red Sea, Israel journeyed through the wilderness to Sinai, where the law was given, then on through the wilderness for forty years to the plains of Moab opposite Jericho. The stages here are the major named stations from Exodus and Numbers in order, not the full forty-two-station list of Numbers 33, which the reader can follow station by station. Debate note: the precise modern locations of many stations are debated; this entry gives Scripture's names and order, not modern identifications.
Significance: The wilderness is where a freed people learn to trust daily bread, law, and God's presence before they can inherit the land.
RelatedEvents: The Golden Calf; The Ten Commandments

Summary: From the wilderness of Paran, Moses sent twelve men to explore Canaan. They went up through the Negev as far as Hebron and the Valley of Eshcol, where they cut a cluster of grapes, then returned after forty days. Ten reported fear; Caleb and Joshua urged trust; Israel refused and was sentenced to forty years in the wilderness. Note: this was a reconnaissance mission, not a migration; it is included because it has a route, a destination, and a return, and its report changed Israel's journey. The Valley of Eshcol has no place entry, so it is named in this summary but not listed as a stage.
Significance: The spies' report is the turning point of the wilderness: unbelief at the border costs a generation the land.
RelatedStories: The Twelve Spies and Israel's Unbelief

Stages: Shittim; Jordan River; Gilgal; Jericho; Ai; Gibeon; Lachish; Hazor
Scripture: Joshua 1:1-18; Joshua 3:1-17; Joshua 6:1-27; Joshua 8:1-35; Joshua 10:1-43; Joshua 11:1-23
Summary: After Moses's death Joshua led Israel from Shittim across the Jordan to Gilgal, took Jericho and Ai, secured Gibeon's surrender, defeated the southern coalition, and then struck the northern coalition as far as Hazor. The stages follow Joshua's campaign order in broad outline; the book names many more towns taken in each campaign, and this entry does not list every one.
Significance: The conquest fulfills the land promise while showing that victory depends on obedience, not numbers.

Summary: Israel left Shittim, camped by the Jordan, and crossed on dry ground as the priests carrying the ark stood in the river. Twelve stones from the riverbed were set up at Gilgal as a memorial. This crossing is the opening movement of the conquest and is listed separately because it is a distinct river-crossing journey with its own memorial.
Significance: The Jordan crossing mirrors the Red Sea: the new generation enters the land the way the old generation left Egypt.

Summary: Finding no inheritance secured for them, the tribe of Dan sent five men to spy out the land; they found Laish, a quiet and unsuspecting town, and the tribe migrated there with their families, renamed it Dan, and set up Micah's idol. Laish is the town later called Dan, so Dan is given as the final stage; the text names no stops between Eshtaol and Laish.
Significance: Dan's migration shows settlement by violence and idolatry rather than by trusting God's allotment.

Stages: Shiloh; Aphek; Ashdod; Gath; Ekron; Beth-shemesh; Kiriath-jearim; Jerusalem
Summary: Captured by the Philistines at Aphek, the ark passed through Ashdod, Gath, and Ekron as plagues followed it, was returned to Beth-shemesh, and rested twenty years at Kiriath-jearim. David then brought it up to Jerusalem with sacrifices and dancing. The stages span decades and several custodians; they trace the ark, not a single party's road.
Significance: The ark's road teaches reverence: God's presence cannot be captured, managed, or carried carelessly.

Summary: Samuel judged Israel year by year on a circuit from his home at Ramah to Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpah, then returned to Ramah, where his house was and where he built an altar. The text gives the circuit towns but not the order he visited them each year, so the stages list the towns rather than a fixed itinerary.
Significance: Samuel's circuit made justice and worship reachable: the judge came to the people instead of waiting for them to come to him.

Journey: Ruth and Naomi's Journey to Bethlehem
Summary: After ten years in Moab, Naomi set out to return to Bethlehem when she heard God had visited his people with bread. Orpah turned back, but Ruth clung to her, saying Naomi's people would be her people and Naomi's God her God. The text names no stops on the road.
Significance: Ruth's road home is loyalty made visible: a foreign widow walks into Israel's story and toward David's line.

Summary: A Levite living in the hill country of Ephraim traveled to Bethlehem to bring back his concubine, then set out for home late in the day and stopped for the night at Gibeah of Benjamin, where the night ended in outrage and murder. The text names no other stops. This entry records the route factually and briefly; it does not retell the crime in detail.
Significance: The journey is a grim marker of the judges' refrain: in those days there was no king, and everyone did what was right in his own eyes.

Stages: Gibeah; Ramah; Gath; Adullam; Keilah; Ziph; Maon
Summary: Hunted by Saul, David fled from Gibeah to Samuel at Ramah, took consecrated bread at Nob (named here in the summary; Nob has no place entry, so it is not a stage), feigned madness before Achish at Gath, gathered outcasts at the cave of Adullam, rescued Keilah, and kept moving through Ziph and Maon as Saul closed in. The stages follow the narrative's named towns in order; David moved more often than this list shows.
Significance: The fugitive years forge the king: David refuses twice to kill Saul, trusting God to give the kingdom rather than seizing it.

Summary: After Saul's death David asked God where to go and was told to go up to Hebron. He moved there with his two wives and his men with their households, and the men of Judah anointed him king over Judah at Hebron. The text names no stops between Ziklag and Hebron.
Significance: Hebron begins David's kingship in Judah seven years before all Israel crowns him in Jerusalem.

Journey: Samson's Journeys to Timnath and Gaza
Summary: Samson went down from Zorah to Timnath to see a Philistine woman, and later went to Gaza, where he tore the city gates from their posts and carried them toward Hebron. The two trips are combined here because both trace Samson's repeated crossings into Philistine country; the text does not date or fully order them against each other.
Significance: Samson's roads run toward entanglement: strength given for deliverance is spent on personal desire until it is lost and restored.

Summary: After announcing drought, Elijah hid by the brook Cherith, where ravens fed him. When the brook dried up, God sent him to Zarephath in Sidonian country, where a widow shared her last meal and her son was later raised from death. The text names no stops between Cherith and Zarephath.
Significance: God provides through the unlikely: a drought, ravens, and a foreign widow's jar become the stage for resurrection.

Summary: Fleeing Jezebel, Elijah left his servant at Beersheba, walked into the wilderness, and after forty days and forty nights reached Horeb, the mountain of God. There God passed by not in wind, earthquake, or fire, but in a still small voice, and sent Elijah back with new commissions. Horeb is another name for the Sinai region; Mount Sinai is given as the stage, and the wilderness stops are not named.
Significance: At the mountain of the law, a burned-out prophet learns God is not only in the spectacular, and is sent back to work.

Summary: Naaman, commander of Syria's army and a leper, traveled to Israel with a letter from his king and gifts, seeking healing. Directed to Elisha, he at first refused to wash in the Jordan, then obeyed and was cleansed. The stages give the journey's endpoints; the Jordan washing is named in the summary, and Samaria stands for the Israelite capital where Elisha was found.
Significance: Healing comes by humble obedience, not by status: a foreign general must wash like anyone else.

Journey: The Shunammite's Journey to Mount Carmel
Summary: When her son died suddenly, the Shunammite woman saddled a donkey and rode to Elisha on Mount Carmel, refusing to explain herself to Gehazi and holding fast to Elisha until he came back with her and raised the boy. The text names no stops on the ride. The woman has no people profile, so Travelers is left blank rather than inventing one.
Significance: A mother's urgent ride becomes a picture of stubborn faith: she will not settle for a staff sent ahead; she wants the prophet himself.

Summary: Jonah first fled toward Tarshish, boarding a ship at Joppa; after the storm and the great fish, God spoke a second time, and Jonah went to Nineveh and preached that the city would be overthrown in forty days. Nineveh repented. Tarshish has no place entry and its location is debated, so it is named here as the intended flight, not listed as a stage; the stages give the journey Jonah actually completed.
Significance: Jonah's road runs from refusal to reluctant obedience, and exposes a prophet who wants mercy for himself but not for his enemies.

Journey: The Queen of Sheba's Visit to Jerusalem
Summary: Hearing of Solomon's fame concerning the name of the LORD, the queen of Sheba came to Jerusalem with a very great train, camels bearing spices, gold, and precious stones, to test him with hard questions. She found his wisdom greater than the report, blessed the LORD, and returned to her own land. The text names no stops on either leg.
Significance: A foreign queen's visit shows Solomon's wisdom drawing the nations, and foreshadows the nations coming to seek God's King.

Summary: In the third year of Jehoiakim, Nebuchadnezzar besieged Jerusalem and carried off some of the vessels of God's house along with young men of royal and noble birth, including Daniel. Daniel was trained in Babylonian learning yet kept himself undefiled. The text names no stops on the deportation march.
Significance: Exile begins Daniel's lifelong witness: faithfulness in a foreign court without compromise or withdrawal.

Summary: After Jerusalem fell, Nebuzaradan carried the people into exile, and the leaders were taken to Nebuchadnezzar at Riblah for judgment before the people were marched to Babylon. The stages follow the narrative's named points; the text does not trace the marching route in detail.
Significance: The exile is judgment with a promise attached: the same prophets who announced it also promised return.
RelatedStories: Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile

Summary: Under Cyrus's decree, Zerubbabel and Jeshua led the first return of exiles from Babylon to Jerusalem with the temple vessels, rebuilt the altar, and laid the temple foundations amid both joy and weeping. The text names no stops on the return road.
Significance: The first return turns Cyrus's decree into worship: an altar before a temple, and foundations before walls.
RelatedStories: Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile

Summary: In the seventh year of Artaxerxes, Ezra the scribe led a second group of exiles from Babylon to Jerusalem, gathering at the river Ahava for fasting and prayer before the journey (Ahava has no place entry, so it is named here and not listed as a stage). Ezra carried silver, gold, and vessels for the temple and delivered the king's commissions. The text gives the journey's length as about four months but names no intermediate stops.
Significance: Ezra's return is a journey of the Book: a scribe who has set his heart to study, practice, and teach the law leads God's people home.

Summary: Nehemiah, cupbearer to Artaxerxes at Susa, wept over Jerusalem's broken walls and asked leave to go and rebuild. The king sent him with letters and an escort, and Nehemiah reached Jerusalem and inspected the walls by night before announcing the work. The text names no stops on the road from Susa.
Significance: Nehemiah's journey turns grief into masonry: prayer in the palace becomes a wall in fifty-two days.

Summary: After Gedaliah's murder, the remnant in Judah refused Jeremiah's warning and forced him and Baruch to go with them into Egypt, settling at Tahpanhes. There Jeremiah prophesied that Nebuchadnezzar would set his throne over Egypt. The text names Tahpanhes as the destination and no stops on the way.
Significance: The forced journey is the remnant repeating Israel's oldest mistake: fleeing to Egypt against God's word.
RelatedStories: Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile

Summary: Wise men from the east came to Jerusalem asking where the King of the Jews was born, were directed by Herod's scribes to Bethlehem, and followed the star to the house where the child was. Warned in a dream, they returned to their own country by another way. Matthew does not name their homeland, so no origin stage is given; the Magi have no people profiles, so Travelers is left blank.
Significance: The first Gentiles to seek Jesus come by starlight and Scripture together, and Herod's court shows the opposite response.

Journey: Joseph and Mary's Journey to Bethlehem
Travelers: Joseph, Husband of Mary; Mary, Mother of Jesus
Summary: Because of Caesar's decree that all the world be taxed, Joseph went up from Nazareth in Galilee to Bethlehem, the city of David, with Mary, who was great with child. There she gave birth to her firstborn son and laid him in a manger. Luke names no stops on the road.
Significance: The census road fulfills Micah's promise: the Messiah is born in Bethlehem because an empire counted its subjects.
RelatedPeople: Joseph, Husband of Mary; Mary, Mother of Jesus

Travelers: Joseph, Husband of Mary; Mary, Mother of Jesus
Summary: Warned in a dream that Herod would seek the child's life, Joseph took Mary and the child by night and departed into Egypt, where they stayed until Herod's death. Matthew names no Egyptian town and no stops on the flight.
Significance: The flight replays Israel's story in miniature: the Son goes down into Egypt and will be called back out.
RelatedPeople: Joseph, Husband of Mary; Mary, Mother of Jesus

Travelers: Joseph, Husband of Mary; Mary, Mother of Jesus
Summary: After Herod's death Joseph was told in a dream to return to Israel, but hearing Archelaus reigned in Judea, he withdrew by divine warning into Galilee and settled at Nazareth. Matthew names no stops on the return road.
Significance: The return completes the Bethlehem-Egypt-Nazareth arc and settles Jesus in the town he will be named from.
RelatedPeople: Joseph, Husband of Mary; Mary, Mother of Jesus

Stages: Nazareth; Cana; Capernaum; Bethsaida; Chorazin; Magdala
Summary: After John's arrest Jesus left Nazareth and made Capernaum his base, teaching in synagogues and healing through the towns and villages of Galilee, including Cana, Bethsaida, Chorazin, and Magdala. The stages list the named Galilean towns of his ministry in narrative order; the Gospels describe a circuit of repeated visits, not a single one-way road, and this entry does not claim a fixed itinerary.
Significance: Galilee becomes the classroom of the kingdom: parables, healings, and callings cluster around these lakeside towns.
RelatedEvents: The Feeding of the Five Thousand; Jesus Calms the Storm

Journey: Jesus's Journey to Tyre, Sidon, and the Decapolis
Summary: Jesus withdrew to the region of Tyre and Sidon, where he healed the Syrophoenician woman's daughter, then returned through the Decapolis, healing the deaf and feeding the four thousand. The stages follow Mark's regional order; the text names towns within the Decapolis only in general terms.
Significance: The journey pushes the kingdom beyond Israel's borders: mercy crosses into Gentile country before the cross.

Summary: Jesus took his disciples into the region of Caesarea Philippi, at the far north of Israel's territory, and asked them who they said he was. Peter confessed him as the Christ, and Jesus began to speak plainly of his coming suffering. The text names no stops on the way north.
Significance: At the edge of the land, the question of Jesus's identity is asked most plainly, and the answer turns the road toward Jerusalem.

Summary: When the days drew near for him to be taken up, Jesus set his face to go to Jerusalem. Luke's travel narrative traces him through Samaritan villages, past Jericho where he met Zacchaeus, up to Bethany, and into Jerusalem for the final week. The stages follow Luke's regional sequence; the narrative includes many teachings and healings along the way that this route entry does not retell.
Significance: The final road is deliberate: Jesus walks toward the cross he has predicted, not away from it.

Summary: On the day of the resurrection, two disciples walked from Jerusalem to Emmaus, about seven miles away, discussing all that had happened. A stranger joined them, opened the Scriptures, and was recognized in the breaking of bread, and they hurried back to Jerusalem the same hour. The other disciple is unnamed in Luke, so only Cleopas is listed as a traveler.
Significance: The Emmaus road is how the risen Jesus is recognized: not at first by sight, but by Scripture and the breaking of bread.

Journey: The Disciples' Journey to Galilee after the Resurrection
Summary: After the resurrection the risen Jesus told the women to tell his brothers to go into Galilee, and there on a mountain the eleven saw him, worshipped, and received the commission to make disciples of all nations. Matthew does not name the mountain, so no mountain stage is given.
Significance: Galilee closes the circle: the place of calling becomes the place of commissioning to the whole world.

Summary: After Stephen's death a great persecution scattered the Jerusalem church through Judea and Samaria, and those who were scattered preached the word wherever they went, reaching Phoenicia (named here; Phoenicia has no place entry, so it is not a stage), Cyprus, and Antioch. Philip's work in Samaria belongs to this scattering. The stages give the named destinations in Acts' order.
Significance: Persecution becomes propagation: the scattering plants the church beyond Jerusalem for the first time.

Summary: Acts traces the gospel from Jerusalem through Judea and Samaria to the ends of the earth: Pentecost, the mission to Samaria and Antioch, the journeys to Cyprus and through the empire, and finally Paul preaching in Rome. This entry is a composite arc, not a single trip; the individual journeys that make it up have their own entries, and this one names only the arc's landmarks.
Significance: The spread fulfills Acts 1:8 in stages: Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria, and the ends of the earth, ending with Paul in Rome.

Summary: Saul, breathing threats against the disciples, set out from Jerusalem for Damascus with letters to arrest believers there. Near Damascus the risen Jesus appeared to him in light, and Saul, blinded, was led into the city, where Ananias baptized him and his sight returned. The text names no stops on the road. Paul's profile covers Saul before and after conversion, so Paul is listed as the traveler.
Significance: The Damascus road is the sharpest conversion in the New Testament: the persecutor becomes the apostle to the Gentiles.

Journey: Paul's Early Travels in Arabia and to Jerusalem
Summary: After his conversion Paul went away into Arabia and returned to Damascus, then after three years went up to Jerusalem to visit Peter and stayed fifteen days. Galatians gives the sequence but no Arabian town and no road details, so only the three named points are given as stages, in order, with Damascus appearing as both start and return point in the summary rather than as a repeated stage.
Significance: Paul's early years show a gospel received by revelation, tested in obscurity, and only then brought to Jerusalem's apostles.

Journey: Barnabas's Journey to Tarsus and Back
Summary: When the church at Antioch grew, Barnabas was sent to encourage it; seeing God's grace there, he went on to Tarsus to look for Saul and brought him back to Antioch, where the two taught together for a whole year. The stages give the out-and-back route; the return leg to Antioch is the journey's endpoint.
Significance: Barnabas's errand to Tarsus recruits the apostle to the Gentiles: encouragement becomes partnership.

Summary: When Agabus prophesied a great famine, the disciples at Antioch determined to send relief to the brothers living in Judea, sending their gift by the hands of Barnabas and Saul. The text names no stops on the road to Jerusalem.
Significance: The first Gentile church's first gift runs toward Jerusalem: grace received becomes relief sent.

Journey: Peter and John's Journey to Samaria
Summary: When the apostles at Jerusalem heard Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John, who prayed for the new believers to receive the Holy Spirit and preached in many Samaritan villages on the way back. The text names no villages on the return.
Significance: Peter and John's visit seals the Samaritan mission: the Spirit falls beyond Jerusalem's old boundaries.

Journey: Peter's Mission to Lod, Joppa, and Caesarea
Summary: Peter traveled through the coastal towns, healing Aeneas at Lydda (listed here as Lod, the place entry's name) and raising Tabitha at Joppa, then was summoned to Caesarea, where he preached to Cornelius's household and saw Gentiles receive the Holy Spirit. The stages follow Acts' order; the journey's turning point is the Caesarea household, not the road itself.
Significance: Peter's coastal road breaks the Gentile barrier: the gospel reaches a Roman household before any council approves it.

Journey: Philip's Mission from Samaria to Caesarea
Summary: Philip preached Christ in Samaria, was directed to the desert road from Jerusalem to Gaza, where he met and baptized the Ethiopian official, and was then found at Azotus (Ashdod in the place list), preaching through the towns until he reached Caesarea. The stages follow Acts' sequence; Philip's profile covers both his apostolic and evangelistic work, so Philip is listed as the traveler.
Significance: Philip's road runs from a city revival to a desert chariot to a coastal home: the gospel keeps moving outward.

Journey: The Ethiopian Official's Return to Ethiopia
Summary: The Ethiopian official, treasurer to Candace, had come to Jerusalem to worship and was returning home reading Isaiah when Philip joined his chariot, explained the passage about the suffering servant, and baptized him at water by the road. The official went on his way rejoicing. He has no people profile, so Travelers is left blank rather than inventing one.
Significance: A single chariot ride carries Isaiah's servant song to Africa: the gospel reaches Ethiopia through one reader.

Journey: The Jerusalem Council Delegates' Return to Antioch
Summary: After the council decided Gentile believers need not be circumcised, the apostles sent Paul, Barnabas, Judas Barsabbas, and Silas back to Antioch with the council's letter. The church rejoiced at the encouragement, and Judas and Silas, themselves prophets, strengthened the brothers. The text names no stops on the return road.
Significance: The delegates' road carries the council's decision home: Gentile freedom is settled by letter, not left to rumor.

Journey: Barnabas and Mark's Journey to Cyprus
Summary: After parting from Paul over John Mark, Barnabas took Mark and sailed to Cyprus, his homeland, to continue the work there. Acts names Cyprus as the destination but no Cypriot town on this trip, so only the island is given as a stage.
Significance: A sharp disagreement becomes a second mission: Barnabas's encouragement gives Mark a road back into ministry.

Stages: Antioch; Salamis; Paphos; Perga; Antioch in Pisidia; Iconium; Lystra; Derbe; Attalia
Summary: Sent out by the Antioch church, Paul and Barnabas sailed to Cyprus, preached at Salamis and Paphos, crossed to Perga where John Mark left them, then traveled inland to Antioch in Pisidia, Iconium, Lystra, and Derbe, appointing elders in each church on the way back before sailing home to Antioch. The port of Seleucia has no place entry, so it is not listed as a stage; the return leg retraced the inland towns and is not repeated in the stage list.
Significance: The first journey proves the pattern: synagogue preaching, Gentile response, Jewish opposition, and churches left behind with elders.

Stages: Antioch; Derbe; Lystra; Troas; Neapolis; Philippi; Amphipolis; Apollonia; Thessalonica; Berea; Athens; Corinth; Cenchrea; Ephesus; Caesarea
Summary: After the Jerusalem council, Paul and Silas revisited the churches of the first journey, were joined by Timothy, were forbidden to preach in Asia and Bithynia, and crossed from Troas to Macedonia after the vision of the Macedonian man. They planted churches at Philippi, Thessalonica, and Berea, preached at Athens, spent eighteen months at Corinth, touched at Ephesus and Caesarea, and returned to Antioch. The stages follow Acts' order; the overland stretches between named towns are not traced town by town.
Significance: The second journey carries the gospel into Europe: Philippi's jailer, Berea's examiners, Athens's philosophers, and Corinth's church.

Stages: Antioch; Galatia; Phrygia; Ephesus; Macedonia; Achaia; Troas; Assos; Mitylene; Chios; Samos; Miletus; Rhodes; Patara; Tyre; Ptolemais; Caesarea; Jerusalem
Summary: Paul traveled through Galatia and Phrygia strengthening the disciples, spent over two years teaching at Ephesus, revisited Macedonia and Achaia to collect the offering and encourage the churches, then sailed back through Troas, Miletus (where he farewelled the Ephesian elders), and the Levantine ports to Jerusalem. Macedonia appears once in the stage list although Paul crossed it twice; the return leg retraced it. The stages follow Acts' named points in order.
Significance: The third journey is the longest and most settled: Ephesus becomes a base, and the farewell at Miletus looks toward Jerusalem and bonds.

Stages: Caesarea; Sidon; Myra; Cnidus; Fair Havens; Clauda; Melita; Syracuse; Rhegium; Puteoli; Appii Forum; Three Taverns; Rome
Summary: As a prisoner appealing to Caesar, Paul sailed from Caesarea under Julius, changed ships at Myra, was driven by a storm past Cnidus and Fair Havens, was shipwrecked on Malta (listed here as Melita, the place entry's name), wintered there, and sailed on through Syracuse, Rhegium, and Puteoli to Rome, where brethren met him at Appii Forum and Three Taverns. The stages follow Acts' ports in order; the storm's drift is summarized, not charted.
Significance: The voyage ends Acts where it aimed from the start: Paul preaching the kingdom in Rome, unhindered.

Summary: Aquila and Priscilla, tentmakers expelled from Rome by Claudius, met Paul at Corinth and traveled with him as far as Ephesus, where they stayed and hosted a church. Later they were back in Rome, where Paul greets them and the church in their house. The stages compress two moves across several years; the text does not trace the roads between these cities.
Significance: A working couple's moves become missionary infrastructure: homes and workshops that host churches in three cities.

Journey: Apollos's Journey to Ephesus and Achaia
Summary: Apollos, an eloquent Alexandrian mighty in the Scriptures, came to Ephesus, where Priscilla and Aquila explained the way of God more accurately to him. Encouraged by the brothers, he crossed into Achaia, where he vigorously refuted opponents and helped believers. The text names no stops between these points.
Significance: Apollos's road shows the value of being teachable: eloquence corrected becomes a powerful ministry in Achaia.

Summary: When Paul could no longer bear separation from the Thessalonian church, he sent Timothy from Athens to establish and exhort them in their faith amid affliction. Timothy returned with good news of their faith and love. The text names the sending city and the destination, not the road between them.
Significance: Timothy's errand is pastoral care at a distance: a young coworker carries encouragement to a persecuted church.

Journey: Titus's Mission to Corinth and Crete
Summary: Titus carried Paul's letters and encouragement between Paul and Corinth, bringing back news of the Corinthians' repentance, and later Paul left Titus in Crete to set in order what remained and appoint elders in every town. The two assignments are combined here because both are Titus's recorded missions; the text does not trace his roads.
Significance: Titus is Paul's troubleshooter: the man sent where churches need mending and ordering.

Summary: The Philippian church sent Epaphroditus to Rome with their gift for Paul and to minister to his needs. He fell seriously ill nearly to death, recovered, and Paul sent him back carrying the letter to the Philippians. The stages give the two endpoints; the return leg is noted in the summary rather than listed twice.
Significance: Epaphroditus's road is partnership in bodily form: a church's gift walks to Rome in a man who nearly dies delivering it.

Summary: Tychicus, Paul's beloved brother and faithful minister, was sent to carry Paul's letters and news to the churches, including Ephesus, and later to Ephesus again from Rome. The stages give the best-attested endpoints; his roads to Colossae and other churches are named in the letters without itineraries, so they are not listed as stages.
Significance: Tychicus is the letter-carrier of the New Testament: without his roads, the epistles do not reach their churches.

Summary: Onesimus, a slave of Philemon at Colossae, reached Paul in Rome, where he became a believer. Paul sent him back to Philemon with Tychicus, carrying the letter to Philemon and no longer asking that he be received as a slave but as a beloved brother. The stages give the flight and the return's endpoints; the text does not say by what road Onesimus reached Rome.
Significance: Onesimus's road turns flight into reconciliation: the gospel sends a runaway back, not as property, but as a brother.

Summary: Phoebe, a servant of the church at Cenchrea, carried Paul's letter to the Romans to Rome, where Paul asks the church to receive her in a manner worthy of the saints and to help her in whatever she may need. The text names no stops on the journey.
Significance: Phoebe's road carries Romans itself: a deacon's journey delivers the most systematic letter in the New Testament.

Summary: John writes that he was on the island called Patmos for the word of God and the testimony of Jesus when he received the Revelation. Tradition places his exile there from Ephesus under Domitian, but Revelation itself names only Patmos; the Ephesus starting point is traditional, not asserted, and is given here as the customary departure point with that caveat. This was an exile, not a voluntary journey.
Significance: Patmos turns banishment into vision: the exiled apostle receives the book that closes the canon.
